client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time I sit down to work, these memories of her just flood in and I can't concentrate on anything — it's like my brain refuses to cooperate. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change how I feel, but I figured I'd give this a try.
therapist: Thank you for taking that step and showing up today, even with that uncertainty about whether it will help — that kind of courage matters. Grief has a way of catching us off guard, especially in quiet moments when we sit down and our minds finally have space to feel what we've been carrying. I'm wondering, when those memories of your grandmother come flooding in, what does that feel like in your body — is it more like sadness, or something else, like longing or even love mixed in with the pain?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It's hard to describe exactly... it's not just sadness, it's more like this hollow ache, almost like reaching for something that isn't there anymore. Sometimes I'll catch a smell or hear a song she liked and it just hits me in the chest, like a physical weight. I guess there's love in it too, but honestly the love almost makes it worse, because it reminds me of everything I didn't say before she passed.
therapist: That image of reaching for something that isn't there anymore is so vivid and real — it captures something that's hard to put into words, and yet you just did. I notice there's something quietly tender in the way you're describing this, like you're holding it very carefully, and I want to gently stay with what you said about the things you didn't get to say. What feels most unfinished for you — is it something specific you wished she had known, or more of a general sense that there was more between you two that didn't get expressed?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it's both, honestly, but if I had to pick one thing... I never told her that I forgave her for some of the harder years when I was a teenager. We had this distance between us for a long time, and then when things finally started to feel easier between us, she got sick so fast, and now I just carry this worry that she died not knowing we were okay. It's like the reconciliation happened in my heart but I never said it out loud to her, and I don't know if she felt it.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds incredibly heavy — the reconciliation was real, it happened, but it lived inside you without ever getting to land between the two of you out loud. I want to gently offer something to sit with: the softening that happened in your relationship, the way things felt easier between you — do you think she might have felt that shift too, even without the words? Sometimes the people who love us most are reading us in ways we don't realize.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I want to believe that, I really do. But I keep coming back to the fact that she died not knowing I had forgiven her for real, not just going through the motions. And honestly, part of me wonders if I'm just telling myself a comforting story to escape the guilt, because how could she have felt something I never even said out loud?
therapist: The way you're questioning yourself — wondering if hope is just a way to escape the guilt — that's such an honest and painful place to sit, and it tells me how much integrity matters to you. But I want to gently turn that question around: is it possible that the forgiveness being real, even if unspoken, says something true about *you* and the love you had for her, rather than being a story you're hiding behind? What do you think it would mean for you if she *did* sense it — would some part of you be able to let that in, or does the guilt feel like it needs to stay?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That question... it kind of stops me, because part of me does want to believe she sensed it, that the love was there even when I wasn't saying the right things. But then there's this other part that feels like if I let that in, I'm just letting myself off the hook too easily, like I'm rewriting history to feel better. I don't know if I've earned the right to feel okay about it yet.
therapist: That phrase — "earned the right to feel okay" — really stays with me, because it suggests you're holding yourself to a kind of debt that may never feel fully paid off, and grief can keep moving the goalposts on us. In CBT terms, this sounds like a belief worth gently examining: where did the idea come from that feeling peace about something means you're letting yourself off the hook, rather than simply... healing? I'm curious what you think your grandmother would say if she could hear you right now, carrying all of this so carefully — would she want you to keep paying, or something else?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I've thought about that question before, actually, and I know what she would say — she'd probably tell me to stop being so hard on myself, that she'd want me to be happy. But knowing that and actually believing I deserve to act on it are two completely different things, and I think that's where I keep getting stuck. It's like I can hold both things at once — "she would want this for me" and "but I still don't feel like I've done enough" — and they just sit there in tension without resolving.
therapist: You've just named something really important — that gap between *knowing* and *believing* is often where the deepest work lives, and it takes real self-awareness to see it so clearly. That tension you're describing, holding both truths at once without them resolving, isn't a sign that you're stuck forever — it's actually the beginning of being able to work with it. I'm wondering, when you imagine what "doing enough" would actually look like, what would need to happen for that bar to finally feel met — is there anything that could ever satisfy it, or does part of you sense that it might keep shifting?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, when I try to picture what "doing enough" would look like, I draw a blank — like there's no actual finish line I can point to. And yeah, part of me suspects the bar would just move, because it always has. I'll hit something I thought would finally make me feel okay, and then I'm already looking at the next thing I fell short on.
therapist: You've just uncovered something really significant — that there *is* no finish line, and some part of you already knows that, which means the bar moving isn't a failure on your part, it's the nature of the standard itself. This sounds like a pattern that's been with you longer than just this grief, like a voice that's been keeping score for a long time. I'm curious — do you have a sense of where that voice came from, or whose it might sound like?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question kind of stopped me for a second, because honestly... it sounds like my own voice, but the more I think about it, the more it sounds like my dad. He never really said "good job" without a "but" attached to it, like there was always something more I could have done, some way I fell short. I guess I just internalized that so completely that I stopped noticing it wasn't actually mine.
therapist: What you just realized is profound — that the voice keeping score was never really yours to begin with, it was handed to you by someone who couldn't offer approval without a condition attached. I notice something in the way you said that, like the words are calm but there's something underneath that feels a little raw or unsettled, which makes complete sense given what you just uncovered. How does it feel to name that out loud — that this critical voice has roots outside of you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: It feels... strange, honestly. Like, part of me wants to believe that — that it's not really my voice — but another part of me immediately pushes back and says, "Well, you've had it so long, doesn't it kind of belong to you now?" I think that's what feels raw, because if I let go of the idea that this critical voice is just who I am, then I don't really know what's left.
therapist: That fear of "what's left" if you let go of this voice is one of the most honest things a person can say, and it makes complete sense — when something has been part of you for so long, it can feel like removing it would leave a hole rather than make space. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: what if that critical voice isn't *who you are*, but rather something you learned to *survive* in an environment where approval always had a condition — and what's left underneath it might actually be closer to your real self than you've ever had a chance to meet? What do you imagine that person — the one without the constant scorekeeper — might be like?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That's... a nice idea, I guess, but honestly it kind of scares me more than comforts me. Like, if that critical voice developed as some kind of survival mechanism, what does that say about who I've been all this time — was I just performing some learned behavior my whole life? And the person underneath... I genuinely don't know if there's anything there, which might be the most frightening thought I've had in this room.
therapist: The fear you just named — that there might be nothing underneath — is actually one of the most vulnerable and courageous things you could say out loud, and I want to sit with it rather than rush past it. But I'd gently push back on one thing: the fact that you can feel that fear, that you *care* about who you are underneath, that you've been carrying guilt about your grandmother because the love was so real — that's not nothing, that's actually someone with a very alive inner world. What if the uncertainty about who you are isn't emptiness, but simply unfamiliarity — like a room you've never been allowed to walk into?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech
